2245: An operational variable
2246: Self-care questions for the leader
2248: Leader self-care as a preventive measure
2249: Leader self-care is not an “individualistic” topic; it is an operational variable. Exhausted leaders tend to communicate worse, listen less, react with irritation, increase control and reduce emotional availability.
2250: So leaders should model healthy behaviours, take breaks, respect limits, avoid glorifying overwork and normalise seeking help.

2260: These are simple, intentional actions that help a person look after their physical and emotional wellbeing day to day and reduce overload in the short term. Although they are important, they do not replace specialist support when there are signs of risk. They include actions such as:
2261: Encouraging basic routines: sleep, eating, movement
2262: Promoting breaks and moments of rest
2263: Staying connected with people you trust
2264: Using simple regulation strategies: breathing, grounding, relaxing activities
2265: Respecting your own pace (without pressure to “feel better” quickly)
2269: Presence without intrusion, support without control, listening without judgement.
2270: The leader can be a key figure for initial stabilisation, but does not replace clinical or specialist support. Their role is to recognise signs, approach in a human way, reduce additional harm, support practical decisions and refer when necessary. Leading for psychological safety therefore means combining structure and humanity.
2279: Psychological safety is built in daily micro-interactions
2280: In demanding organisational contexts, preventing psychosocial risk does not depend only on formal policies or programmes. It depends, to a large extent, on people’s everyday relational experience at work: how they are heard, treated and supported when something is not right.
2281: The evidence suggests that psychological safety is built in daily micro-interactions, through leaders who are accessible, consistent, responsive and non-punitive, but also through clear, fair and well-organised working conditions.
2282: When structure and humanity come together, people tend to speak up earlier, ask for help with less fear, cooperate better and stay more connected to the team and to the work.
